42. A similar view was held by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Baradakanta vs Registrar Orissa HC, AIR 1974 SC 710 where they quoted with approval Wilmot CJ in Rex vs Almon:

"The arraignment of the Judges, is arraigning the King's justice; it is an impeachment of his wisdom and goodness in the choice of his Judges, and excites in the minds of the people a general dissatisfaction with all judicial determinations, and indisposes their minds to obey them; and whenever men's allegiance to the laws is so fundamentally shaken, it is the most fatal and most dangerous obstruction of justice and, in my opinion, calls out for a more rapid' and immediate redress than- any other obstruction whatsoever; not for the sake of the Judges as private individuals, but because they are the channels by which the King's justice is conveyed to the people. To be impartial, and to be universally thought so are both absolutely necessary for the giving justice that free, open and uninterrupted current, which it has for many ages, found all over this Kingdom 	"

43. Mr Ajmalul Hossain QC, appearing for the petitioner, has referred to the case of Secretary,' Ministry of Finance vs Md Masdar Hossain and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 82 in support of his contention that a Judge once appointed must enjoy unfettered independence both from within and without in his function as a Judge and once a Judge is appointed he can be dealt with only through due process of law. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division in Masdar Hossain s case quoted certain portion from the case of Walter Valente vs Her Majesty the Queen, reported in (1985) 2 RCS 673 which dealt with the independence of Judiciary Their Lordships of the Appellate Division held as under:

"The Independence of the judiciary, as affirmed and declared by Articles 94(4) and 116A, is one of the basic pillars of the Constitution and cannot be demolished, whittled down, curtailed or diminished in any manner whatsoever, except under the existing provisions of the Constitution. It is true that this independence, as emphasised by the learned Attorney-General, is subject to the provisions of the Constitution but we find no provision in the Constitution which curtails, diminishes or otherwise abridges this independence. Articles 115, Article 133 or Article 136 does not give either the Parliament or the President the authority to curtail or diminish the independence of the subordinate judiciary by recourse to subordinate legislation or rules. What cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly. Reverting back to the case of Walter Valente vs Her Majesty the Queen, (1985) 2 RCS 673, we find that the Supreme Court of Canada listed three essential conditions of judicial independence. To cite from the said case, " ..... ,. Security of tenure because of the importance traditionally attached to it, is the first of the essential conditions of judicial independency for purposes of section 11 (d) of the Charter. The essentials of such security are that a Judge be removed only for cause, and that cause be subject to independent review and determination by a process at which the Judge affected is afforded a full opportunity to be heard. The essence of security of tenure for purposes of section 11 (d) is a tenure, whether until an age of retirement, for a fixed term, or for a specific adjudicative task, that is secure against interference by the Executive or other appointing authority in a discretionary or arbitrary manner. (page 675).

44. The third essential condition of judicial independence is institutional independence of the subordinate judiciary, especially from the Parliament and the Executive. It must be free to decide on its own matters of administration bearing directly on the exercise of its judicial functions. The Supreme Court of Canada held and we respectfully agree with the view that judicial control over such matters as assignment of Judges sitting of Courts and Court list is an essential or minimum requirement for institutional Independence. The judiciary must be free from actual or apparent interference or dependence upon especially the executive arm of Government. It must be free from powerful non-governmental interference like pressure from corporate giants business or corporate bodies pressure groups media political pressure etc."

<u>45. It is absurd proposition to say that the judgment speaks of independence of Subordinate Judiciary only. Unless the superior Court is independent, independence of Subordinate Judiciary is an absurdity. Therefore, once Justice Faisal Mahmud Faizee was appointed a Judge of this Court he is entitled to enjoy full independence not only from the interference of the executive wing of the govern merit but from all quarters including media. Any question questioning his appointment as a Judge is bound to shake the confidence of the people in him and this Court as this institution does not function individually rather it functions institutionally and the reports have done the mischief of shaking the confidence of the people in this institution. Once a judge is appointed he can be dealt with only through due process of law and not otherwise.</u>

46. The reports published personal opinion of the reporter’s contemner No.5 based his report on examination of certain witnesses. By the very nature of our investigation in this case which is summary in nature no evidence can be taken. Report does not also refer to any memorandum of evidence recorded by him. Only basis of the report is the portion of the resolution of the Senate quoted in Affidavit-in-opposition. We find on perusal of both the resolutions No. 353 and 362 that there is no reference of any particular student with the roll number.

47. Therefore, portion quoted as above in the banner headline and those portions conveying the idea that Justice Faizee did not pass the LLB Examination or his certificate is forged is unfounded and without any basis and since the reports have shaken the confidence of the people in this Court they constitute gross contempt of this Court. This is more so because there is nothing on record to substantiate that LLB Certificate of Justice Faizee is forged or that he has no LLB Certificate, particularly in view of the facts of Annexures C and D which are the result published in the Gazette and the certificate Annexure E issued by the Chittagong University. Adrriittedly none of them has been cancelled as yet.

48. Now the question posed by Dr Kamal Hossain, the learned Counsel is, whether the respondents who came to possess such a report should suppress it or should they publish it. Our answer is that if the resolutions were published as they are it would not have been a contempt. We want to say further that if a Judge commits a crime any news of such act of the judge will not be a contempt as nobody is above law and law is no respecter of a person.

49. Dr Kamal Hossain submits that sunlight is the greatest disinfectant to any malady and submits that all that has been done by His clients is with a pious motive of avoiding future ill-considered elevations to the Court and for remedial measures of the concerned authority. He has posed questions, as was posed by AM Rosenthal, New York Times Magazine Editor, that how the respondents can tell the people who have a right to know that. "We know but you can't know". He submits that respondents are engaged in making information available to the nation and therefore, if such reporters are punished taking resort to law of contempt of Court it will discourage any news about crimes and social evils. In support of his contention he has relied upon the case of Attorney-General vs BBC reported in (AC) 1981 303. This case and other cases in this line are all relating to prior restraints and we are also of the view that there should not be any prior restraint against publications.

50. It is true that freedom of press is an essential pre-requisite for a successful working of democratic institutions but care is to be taken that such freedom is not abused. It is necessary to safeguard not only the interest of other citizens in so far as their right to reputation is concerned but also of ensuring that freedom of press or speech shall not be used by scheming ruffians as a licence for the purpose of subverting the organised Civil Government of the day. In the case of Schenck vs United States (1919) 249 US 47 Justice Holmes rightly observed, "The most stringent freedom of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theater, and causing a panic. It does not even protect a man from an injunction against uttering words that may have all the effect of force".

<u>51. In our Constitution, Article 39(2) puts a restriction on the freedom of press and made it subject to the law of contempt. We have also considered the leading case on prior restraint i.e. the case of Near vs Minnesota Ex ReI Olson reported in 283 US 696, 697 and we find that even while discouraging prior restraint the American Supreme Court held as follows:</u>

<u>"But it is recognised that punishment for the abuse of the liberty accorded to the press is essential to the protection of the public, and that the common law rules that subject the libeler to responsibility for the public offence, as well as for the private injury, are not abolished by the protection extended in our constitutions. The law of criminal libel rests upon that secure foundation. There is also the conceded authority of Courts to punish for contempt when publications directly tend to prevent the proper discharge of judicial functions"</u>

<u>52. In other words, "liberty of the press" as Lord Mansfield says "consists in printing without any previous licence subject to the consequences of the law". This is to say press is at liberty to publish anything but if any publication is found to be an abuse of such liberty the offender must face the consequences of his temerity. VG Ramachandran in his Book "Contempt of Court" says, right of freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) does not embrace freedom to commit contempt of Court.</u>

<u>53. We may again quote Justice Holmes when he said,</u>

<u>"There is no constitution at right to publish a fact merely because it is true. This law is not for the protection of the person attacked. It is for the protection of the public welfare."</u>

<u>54. Mr Ajmalul Hossain QC rightly argued that unless there is independence of judiciary Article 144 will be only an ornament in the Constitution without any avail to the citizens because if there is no independent Supreme Court to redress grievances it will be futile to have such an Article. It is true that administration of justice has become more complex, crimes have gone beyond proportion and free press can serve as watchdog in fighting against social ills. The press must bring to light the dark aspect of the society but in so doing it cannot scandalise a judge or Court or interfere with the administration of justice.</u>

55. From perusal of the Annexures as referred to the Supplementary Affidavit of the petitioner now we know what has been the effect of these reports in the administration of justice. Some members of the Bar seem to have lost confidence in Justice Faizee. The Hon'ble Chief Justice had to change the list. The institution is being deprived of the service of a sitting judge. The report had so pervading effect on the society as a whole that even a columnist no less than Mr Zafar Iqbal wrote ইদানিং বিচারক শব্দটা বিপদগ্রস্ত শুনলেই জাল মার্কশিটের কথা মনে আসে।

56. We are not concerned with the private injury of Justice Faizee or the petitioner, for that they are at liberty to proceed against the condemners in accordance with law if so advised. We are concerned with the institution and we are also concerned with the embarrassment created in the administration of justice of this Court from the effect of Annexures A and B. We find that these reports have brought this institution into disrepute and they have interfered with the administration of justice of this institution and a serious embarrassment has been created in the functioning of this Court because of the publications, which are not borne by facts or records produced before us.

57. In considering the effect of the reports we are also considering the situation of our people, the rate of literacy in general, their lack of knowledge about the functioning of the Courts and the reverence to which printed matters are held by the ordinary public. In this connection we may refer profitably a portion of the judgment reported in 44 DLR (AD) 309 wherein their Lordships observed as follows:

"However, in a country where the rate of literacy is low and words in print are generally revered the Court may consider what impact a written criticism of Court will have in the minds of public. Similar observation was made in the case of Mcleod vs St Aubun reported in 1899 (AC) 549 where it was pointed out by their Lordships of Privy Council, "But it must be considered that in small colonies, consisting principally of co loured population, the enforcement in proper cases of committal for contempt of Court for attacks on the Court may be absolutely necessary to preserve in such a community the dignity of and respect for the Court".

<u>58. We also do not find any reason in applying the law of contempt to distinguish on the ground of colour but hard reality is that we are yet to achieve a standard when laws of Contempt can be said to have become obsolete. The reports questioned the appointment of Justice Faizee, scandalised him and this Court for which confidence of the people in this Court has been fundamentally shaken and such act of the respondents denigrating this institution must be detested and punished. We hold that the respondents are guilty of gross contempt of the Court. The use of the mark of exclamation after the headline or good intention or motive or truth of the publication is of no consequence.</u>

59. In this connection we want to quote with approval from judgment of Indian Supreme Court inthe case of MR Parashar and others vs Dr Farooq Abdullah and others reported in AIR 1984 (SC) 61 wherein their Lordships held:

"We would also like to remind those who criticise the judiciary that it has no forum from which to defend itself. The legislature can act in defence ofitselffrom the floor of the House. It enjoys privileges which are beyond the reach of law. The executive is all powerful and has ample resources and media at its command to explain its actions and if need be to counter- attack. Those who attack the judiciary must remember that they are attacking an institution which is indispensable for the survival of the rule of law but which has no means of defending itself. In the very nature of things, it cannot engage itself in an open war, nor indulge in releasing contractions. The sword of justice is in the hands of the Goddess of Justice, not in the hands of mortal Judges. Therefore, Judge must receive the due protection of law from unfounded attacks on their character."

60. We want to quote Lord Denning when he said, "All we would ask is that those who criticise us will remember that from the nature of our office, we cannot reply to their criticisms. We cannot enter into public controversy. Still less into political controversy. We must rely on our conduct itself to be its own vindication"

61. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate referred to the story of Hans Christian Andersen "The Emperor's New Suit" and posed a question as to why defect in the system of appointment of judge's should be ignored and those who criticise it should be punished.

<u>62. We want to make it manifest that if a judge is appointed without requisite qualification, the matter is not without a remedy. The very appointment may be challenged for want of proper consultation. The Supreme Judicial Council may be activated for the redress but the judge cannot be dealt with except through due process of law.</u>

<u>63. In this connection, another Bench of this Court already expressed itself in the case of Criminal Miscellaneous Case (Contempt), Case No. 6506 of 2000 State vs Chief Editor Manabjamin and others about this malady suggesting that the recruitment must be made after consultation with the Chief Justice and the full Court. We are, however, not in favour of election in the full Court. The decision should be taken on consensus. In Pakistan, such questions were answered by Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Al-Jehad Trust vs Federation of Pakistan PLD 1996 SC 324 making the following conclusion and directions:</u>

<u>"7. Our conclusion and direction in a nutshell are as under:</u>

<u>(i) The words "after consultation" employed, inter alia, in Article 177 and 193 of the Constitution connote that consultation should be effective, meaningful, purposive, consensus oriented, leaving no room for complaint of arbitrariness or unfair play. The opinion of the Chief Justice of Pakistan and the Chief Justice of a High Court as to the fitness and suitability of a candidate for judgeship is entitled to be accepted in the absence of very sound reasons to be recorded by the President Executive.</u>

<u>(ii) That if the President/Executive appoints a candidate found to be unfit and unsuitable for judgeship by the Chief Justice of -Pakistan and the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned, it will not be a proper exercise of power under the relevant Article of the Constitution.</u>

<u>(iii) That Additional Judges appointed in the High Court against permanent vacancies or if permanent vacancies occur while they are acting as Additional Judges, acquire legitimate expectancy and they are entitled to be considered for permanent appointment upon the expiry of their period of appointment as Additional. Judges and they are entitled to be appointed as such if they are recommended by the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan in the absence of strong valid reason/reasons to be recorded by the Presidentl Executive.</u>

<u>(iv) That the requirement of 10 years practice under Article 193(2)(a) of the Constitution relates to the experience/practice at the Bar and not simpliciter the period of enrolment.</u>

<u>(v) That the simpliciter political affiliation of a candidate for judgeship of the superior Courts may not be a disqualification provided the candidate is of an unimpeachable integrity, having sound knowledge in law and is recommended by the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan.</u>

<u>(vi) That since consultation for the appointment/confirmation of Judge of a Superior Court by the President/ Executive with consulters mentioned in the relevant Articles of the Constitution is mandatory, any appointment/confirmation made without consulting any of the consulters as interpreted above would be violative of the Constitution and, therefore, would be invalid.</u>

<u>We may consider these guidelines and directions while addressing the question of appointment of judges.</u>

64. Historically, no system of selection of judges has yet been proved to be perfect. In the Uriited States of America President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, appoints judges in the Supreme Court. President George Washington chose sound federalists for the Supreme Court. His successors carefully distributed the judicial seats regionally as required by political necessity. The framers did not prescribe any criteria, professional or otherwise, for the choice of justice. Presidents are motivated by three concerns in choosing a nominee: politics, policy and professionalism. The choice of the presidents undergoes the scrutiny of the Senate. Yet in 1872, because of their gross abuse of power, their venality their improper conduct, charges of impeachment were drawn up against Justice Barnard and Justice Albert Cardozo. Cardozo resigned and Barnard was impeached and forever barred from public office.

65. Of the territorial judges who were strictly appointive President Johnson had to remove Benedict from office as a drunkard.

66. The elective system in the State Supreme Court could not also prove to be perfect. Defeat of Chief Justice Lawrence looked like a case where, "a herd of dissatisfied farmers have put an ignorant demagogue in the seat of an able and upright judge". These words were written by an editor of the Albany Law Joumal in 1873 at a time when a new and futile attempt was made to overturn the principle in New York. The writer added:

The people are the worst possible judges of those qualifications essential for a good judge. They could select an orator, an advocate or a debater, as his qualities are palpable and salient; but the qualities of a judge are peculiar, and are seldom appreciated by cursory and general notice. That uncommon, recondite and difficult learning; that power and turn of mind and cast of character called the "judicial", are likely to go unremarked by the non-professional observer. To him the effective advocate seems best fitted to fill the judicial office; but experience has proved that the best advocate is not likely to prove the best judge, as the two functions exact diverse qualifications."

67. But the chief objection to an elective judiciary is the effect it has upon the office; its dignity; its just weight; its hold upon the general confidence.

68. While it may be true that the selection of candidates for judges is generally left to the legal members of the (party) conventions, it is equally true that these legal members are not usually such a class of lawyers as is competent to do anything so important as the making of a judge-young, ambitious men, more familiar with the management of ward caucuses or town meetings than with the conduct of a cause in Court." (History of American Law by Lawrence M Friedman 2nd Edition p 372)

69. Academic qualifications are often considered to be good qualification to make a good Judge but history does not support this contention either. Justice John Marshal having no formal decree in law emerged as one of the best judges in the American Supreme Court. Similarly, Justice Robert Jackson had only one year in the law school yet he tore Frankfufer's Gobiti's 'opinion' to 'shreds' and "handed the Harvard professor a failing grade in front of the whole class and could send Gobit's opinion to the judicial graveyard." (A People S History of the Supreme Court by Peter Irons pages 344, 345.) Our system worked successfully in the past. If it has become unworkable now let us 'identify the factors responsible for the problems and try to remove them.

70. We have also heard the learned Additional Attorney-General and he is of the opinion that the publication in question constitutes gross contempt of this Court and he further submits that if such contempt is allowed to go unpunished it will be difficult for this institution to function. In this connection, he has referred to a passage from the judgment of K Lyer, J. In re S. Mulgaokar, AIR 1978 (SC) 727, 57 which runs as follows:

"A concluding note. I have launched on this long, inconclusive essay in contempt jurisprudence bearing on scandalising the Judges qua Judges, aware that not high falutin rhetoric but hard-headed realism, illumined by constitutional values must set the limit and interpret the statute. It is a disturbing development in our country that the media and some men in the trade of traducement are escalatingly scandalising Judges with flippant or motivated write-ups wearing a pro bono public veil and mood of provocative mock challenge. The Court shall not meditate nor hesitate but shall do stem justice to such professional condemners, not shrink because they are scurrilous, influential or incorrigible."

71. In view of our discussion as above this Rule is made absolute and in view of the gravity of the offence and the manner in which a judge and the Court have been scandalised the respondents Contemner No. (1) Ekramaul Haque Bulbul, reporter of the Daily Prothom Alo. Respondent Contemner No. (2) Masud Milad, reporter of the Daily Prothom Alo. Respondent Contemner No. (3) Matiur Rahman, Editor of the Daily Prothom Alo and Respondent Contemner No. (4) Mahfuz Anam, Publisher of the Daily Prothom Alo are sentenced to pay fine of Taka 1000 (Taka one thousand) each in default to suffer simple imprisonment for one month. Contemner-Respondent Nos. (6) Abed Khan, Editor of the Daily Bhorer Kagoj and Contemner-Respondent No.(7) Saber Hossain Chowdhury, Publisher of the Daily Bhorer Kagoj are also sentenced to pay a fine of Taka 1000 (Taka one thousand) each in default to suffer simple imprisonment for one month.

<u>72. We have taken a lenient view about the sentence in recognition of the past services of the respondents to the nation.</u>

<u>73. Before parting with the judgment we want to observe that the Press and the Bar may formulate some joint guidelines in line with the guidelines as per appendix to the judgment of justice Brennan in the case of Nebraska Press Association vs Stuart reported in 427 US 539 in reporting Court matters. We further like to observe that no communication 'with the Judges of this Court either over telephone or otherwise is permissible except through the Registrar of the Court. The press should not publish news creating unnecessary sensations about Court matters. We further observe that step should be taken to codify the laws of contempt as has been done in India and Pakistan. The High Court Division should either frame its own Contempt Rules or adopt the rules framed by the Appellate Division without further delay.</u>
